refs.ref: Downing, Laura J. 1989. The interaction of tone and intonation in Jita yes/no questions [issue ToC title: 'Tone in Jita questions']. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 19(2) (Fall 1989: The Contribution of African Linguistics to Linguistic Theory, vol. 1): 91-113. Urbana: Department of Linguistics, University of Illinois.

contra.head: A comparative thesis reports a demarcative penultimate accent (intensity peak and lengthening) alongside the tone system
contra.detail: Philippson 1991 (own field notes on Jita, p. 516) surveys the status of the penultimate syllable across East African Bantu (ch. 3.5 'La prééminence de la pénultième', pp. 483-486; typology 3.5.2 from p. 484) and in the per-language annex (p. 502). In the survey he writes: 'quelque chose de très semblable est perceptible en jita et en ruri (groupe VI), où une longueur en syllabe pénultième de mot ressort beaucoup plus qu'une longueur située dans une syllabe précédente (le phénomène n'est d'ailleurs pas propre à la position devant pause absolue, mais également en contexte); une syllabe pénultième brève est également mise en valeur par un léger allongement, mais ici, bien plus nettement devant…

5479.loc: pp. 94-95, sec. 2 'Tone Patterns of Yes/No Questions' (representation (9))
5479.idn: Name in the source: Jita; family in the source: E. Bantu; 'a Lacustrine Bantu language'

tn.quote: Yes/no questions have the same basic tone pattern as the corresponding declaratives, with an intonational high tone 'superimposed' on the basic pattern … As a result, the simple high vs. low tone contrast found on the surface in declaratives becomes a three-way contrast in yes/no questions. … In (la), the declarative, we find only high and low tones (high-toned syllables are marked with an acute accent; low-toned syllables are unmarked). … syllable (= tone-bearing unit) … each syllable after the application of the post-lexical rules, including insertion of default low tones.
tn.cite: Downing, Laura J. 1989. The interaction of tone and intonation in Jita yes/no questions [issue ToC title: 'Tone in Jita questions']. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 19(2) (Fall 1989: The Contribution of African Linguistics to Linguistic Theory, vol. 1): 91-113. Urbana: Department of Linguistics, University of Illinois.
tn.locator: pp. 94-95, sec. 2 'Tone Patterns of Yes/No Questions' (representation (9))
tn.note: Two surface tones, high and low, on the syllable; lows are default-inserted and highs shift one syllable rightward; yes/no questions add a raised register; a phrase-final high falls in declaratives.

5479.cfw: One first-hand description of the tone system, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Downing 1989.

evidence_works.work: Philippson 1991, Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique (Thèse de doctorat d'État, Université Paris 5: 542 pp.; Jita at pp. 72, 132-134, 340-342, 412, 484-486, 502)
evidence_works.note: Jita data are the author's own field notes (Sources, p. 516: 'J'AI UTILISE MES PROPRES NOTES... POUR LES LANGUES SUIVANTES:... - jita, ruri (groupe VI)'; the procedure is stated only generically for the whole set of languages: from a word list and a few verb forms collected in one afternoon up to tens of hours of recording), plus Downing 1988, 'Tonology of noun-modifier phrases in Jita', a paper presented at the 19th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, Boston, listed under Jita in the bibliography (Groupe VI (Suguti), p. 520). Jita is marked '++' (well described) in Table 1 (E 25, groupe VI Suguti, p. 72). Tone-system detail consistent with the entry: three tone patterns on disyllabic nominal stems (BB, BH, HB), p. 412; Meeussen's rule present; displaced association (a H shifts to the following syllable) except that a H on the penultimate or final before absolute pause escapes the shift, pp. 132-133, 485, 502; nominals ending in two unmarked syllables receive a final mark phrase-internally, pp. 133, 340-341. The thesis labels the system 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H' (p. 502) and 'le jita (analysable, lui aussi, comme langue à accent)' (p. 132): this is the author's representational framework (privative marked syllables plus a H melody) applied to almost every language in the survey, not a claim that Jita lacks lexical tone, and does not bear on tone_cls.

tn.quote: Tones: The non-laryngealized High, Mid, and Low tones are written -á, -a, -à; the laryngealized Mid and Low tones are written -aq, -àq. Laryngealization occurs in all finals except -u and -i. (See Appendix 4 for possible syllables.) … Aspirated stops and fricatives only occur non-laryngealized. … The tonal systems of Khàtú and Píjò correspond exactly to Akha and Hani. The low tone is in all of them slightly falling. Some differences in the tones may depend on sandhi rules, which remain to be worked out for Hani, Khàtú, and Píjò.

refs.ref: Stappers, Leo, L. Mulaji & T. Kalela. 1980. Textes kanyok. Africana Linguistica 8 (Annales MRAC 101): 199-226.

5481.idn: Name in the source: kanyok; the statement concerns a variety of this language (kanyôk de l'ouest (bwiin kanyôk, Western Kanyok))

tn.quote: L'absence d'un signe sur une voyelle ou sur des voyelles successives Indique qu'el le(s) porte(nt) un ton haut. L'accent grave marque un ton bas. L'accent circonflexe ou la séquence "sans signe" suîvied'un accent grave symbolise un ton descendant. Le trait vertical indique l'abaissement du ton haut par rapport au ton haut immédiatement précédent. L'accent grave flottant, enfin, marque un ton descendant postérieur et il est en distribution complémentaire avec le ton haut abaissé.
tn.translation: The absence of a sign on a vowel or on successive vowels indicates that it/they bear a high tone. The grave accent marks a low tone. The circumflex, or the sequence 'no sign' followed by a grave accent, symbolises a falling tone. The vertical stroke indicates the lowering of the high tone relative to the immediately preceding high tone. The floating grave accent, finally, marks a posterior falling tone and is in complementary distribution with the lowered high tone.
tn.cite: Stappers, Leo, L. Mulaji & T. Kalela. 1980. Textes kanyok. Africana Linguistica 8 (Annales MRAC 101): 199-226.
tn.locator: Introduction, 'Les tons', p. 202
tn.note: Western Kanyok texts mark high, low and falling tones on every vowel, plus a lowered (downstepped) high after a high and a floating final falling tone in complementary distribution with it.

5481.cfw: One first-hand description of the tone system, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

5482.idn: Name in the source: dialek Melayu Satun (Satun Malay); family in the source: dialek Melayu (a Malay dialect; 'aspek fonologinya mirip dengan dialek Kedah'; dialek Melayu Langkawi and dialek Melayu Satun 'adalah serumpun'); the statement concerns a variety of this language

tn.quote: Menurut Court (dalam Gandour 1979), kemasukan nada dalam bahasa Melayu terutama DST lebih kepada nada naik turun / / terutama di akhir suku kata yang terbuka. Manakala bagi nada tinggi / / di tempat-tempat lain. … Sementara bagi vokal panjang, bunyi aspirasi dan bernada tidak akan ditemui dalam DML. Mudahnya, ciri ini tiada pada DML. … Begitu juga bagi vokal panjang dan nada, kedua-duanya hadir pada bahasa Thai tetapi tidak pada DSL dan DST. Ini bermakna masyarakat Satun banyak meminjam leksikal dari Thai. Yang jelasnya, leksikal ini dipinjam bersama ciri fonologinya.
tn.translation: According to Court (in Gandour 1979), the tone that enters Malay, especially DST [Thai Satun dialect], is mostly the rising-falling tone / ˆ/, especially on open final syllables, and the high tone / ´/ elsewhere. … As for long vowels, aspirated sounds and toned sounds, they will not be found in DML [Langkawi Malay dialect]. Simply, these features are absent in DML. … Likewise for long vowels and tone: both are present in Thai but not in DSL and DST. This means the Satun community borrows much lexicon from Thai. Clearly, this lexicon is borrowed together with its phonological features.
tn.cite: Nor Hashimah Jalaluddin, Adriana Santa Tinggom, Siti Noraini Hamzah & Hayati Lateh. 2019. Penyebaran dialek Melayu Satun di Langkawi dan di Thai: satu kajian perbandingan berasaskan Geographic Information System (GIS) [The distribution of Satun Malay dialect in Langkawi and Thai: a comparative study based on GIS]. GEMA Online Journal of Language Studies 19(1):77-96.
tn.locator: p. 89 (section 'NADA (TONE)') and p. 91
tn.note: No tone in Langkawi (Kedah) Malay; in the Satun varieties Thai loanwords keep their Thai tones (rise-fall on open final syllables, high elsewhere) and a few Malay words take them among bilinguals.

5485.idn: Name in the source: Likpakpaln; family in the source: Mabia family, subgroup Mabia East (Bodomo, 2020)

tn.quote: Three level tones (high, mid, and low) are identified in the tonal system of Likpakpaln. The syllable is the tone‑bearing unit in Likpakpaln and can be a vowel or a syllabic nasal. … the involvement of the M tone phenomenon in lexical distinctions in Likpakpaln is far less elaborate compared to the role of the high and low tones. … Beyond the three tone levels, downstep has also been reported in Likpakpaln (Schwarz, 2007). … The non‑systematic and indeterminate status of contour tones in Likpakpaln thus supports its classification as a register tone language.

refs.ref: Lekebai, Oscar. 2025. Phonologie du Kwó. Mémoire de Master, Université de Yaoundé I (Faculté des Arts, Lettres et Sciences Humaines; dir. Joseph Mbongue). 134 pp. hdl:20.500.12177/13789 (DICAMES).

5486.loc: Conclusion générale, p. 93; same finding in ch. 4 conclusion, p. 76, surface list sect. 4-1 p. 70
5486.idn: Name in the source: kwó; family in the source: langue de la famille adamawa du groupe Mbùm (mbum-sud); niger-kordofan, niger-congo, Adamaoua oubanguien, Adamaoua, mbum, mbum-sud

tn.quote: Le chapitre 4 quant à lui nous a présenté les tons qui meublent le kwó. Ainsi, sur le plan phonétique, nous constatons que la langue possède 5 tons dont 3 tons ponctuels et 2 tons modulés. Sur le plan phonologique cependant, l‟étude révèle 2 tons à savoir le ton haut et le ton bas. Le ton moyen et les tons modulés sont issus des processus phonologiques et ne s‟inscrivent par conséquent pas dans le tableau tonémique du kwó. Pour finir, nous avons vu que, le kwó a 3 fonctions tonales à savoir: une fonction distinctive, une fonction grammaticale, une fonction lexicale.
tn.translation: Chapter 4 presented the tones found in Kwó. On the phonetic level we find that the language has 5 tones, 3 level tones and 2 contour tones. On the phonological level, however, the study reveals 2 tones, namely the high tone and the low tone. The mid tone and the contour tones result from phonological processes and therefore do not belong to the tonemic chart of Kwó. Finally, we saw that Kwó has 3 tonal functions: a distinctive, a grammatical and a lexical function.
tn.cite: Lekebai, Oscar. 2025. Phonologie du Kwó. Mémoire de Master, Université de Yaoundé I (Faculté des Arts, Lettres et Sciences Humaines; dir. Joseph Mbongue). 134 pp. hdl:20.500.12177/13789 (DICAMES).
tn.locator: Conclusion générale, p. 93; same finding in ch. 4 conclusion, p. 76, surface list sect. 4-1 p. 70
tn.note: Two phonemic tones, high and low, every vowel bearing a tone; surface mid, rising and falling are derived (contours = high-low sequences, mid = a lowered second high); floating tones posited.

refs.ref: Barreteau, Daniel & Yves Le Bleis. 1990. Lexique mafa: langue de la famille tchadique parlée au Cameroun. (Études tchadiques, Monographies.) Paris: Éditions de l'ORSTOM / Librairie Orientaliste Paul Geuthner. 473 pp. IRD fdi:34119.

5490.idn: Name in the source: mafa; family in the source: famille tchadique, branche centrale; groupe mafa

tn.quote: Il Y a une opposition de deux tons ponctuels haut / bas. Le ton haut (H) est marqué par un accent, le ton bas (B) est non-marqué: vézay "épervier" vézay "derrière" … Il y a très peu de paires minimales de ce genre dans le lexique. Considérant les deux derniers tons d'un nom, on peut distinguer des schèmes tonals isotones (H-H, B-B) ou hétérotone (H-B). Lexicalement, aucune schème ne se termine par une séquence bas-haut (B-H). Dans certaines constructions grammaticales apparait un ton modulé bas-haut (BH) sur la dernière syllabe.
tn.translation: There is an opposition of two level (punctual) tones, high / low. The high tone (H) is marked with an accent, the low tone (B) is unmarked: vézay 'sparrowhawk' / vezay 'behind' … There are very few minimal pairs of this kind in the lexicon. Considering the last two tones of a noun, one can distinguish isotone (H-H, L-L) or heterotone (H-L) tonal schemes. Lexically, no scheme ends in a low-high (L-H) sequence. In certain grammatical constructions a modulated low-high (LH) tone appears on the last syllable.
tn.cite: Barreteau, Daniel & Yves Le Bleis. 1990. Lexique mafa: langue de la famille tchadique parlée au Cameroun. (Études tchadiques, Monographies.) Paris: Éditions de l'ORSTOM / Librairie Orientaliste Paul Geuthner. 473 pp. IRD fdi:34119.
tn.locator: p.20, 'Éléments phonologiques' sec. 5 'Les tons'
tn.note: Two level tones, high and low, with a tone on each syllable; few lexical minimal pairs; a rising low-high surfaces only on final syllables in certain grammatical constructions.

refs.ref: Bickmore, Lee. 2007. High-toned Mora Insertion Between Onsetless Morphemes in Cilungu. In Doris L. Payne & Jaime Peña (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 37th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 88-95. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project.

5491.idn: Name in the source: Cilungu; family in the source: Bantu; the statement concerns a variety of this language

tn.quote: An acute accent indicates High tone, a grave accent indicates Low tone, and a raised exclamation point indicates downstep. The <+H> found in underlying representations indicates a “Melodic High” tone … Since only High tones are “active” in Cilungu in the sense of having rules which insert, delete and spread them, I assume an underlying tonal contrast of H vs. Ø. Furthermore, I assume that the tone bearing unit in the language is the mora.

5496.prule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root (the C1/sigma-1 position), which is the position of maximal phonemic contrast.
5496.quote: The first root syllable in Mpyemo is prominent. Contrast is at its maximum in the first root syllable and decreases as one moves rightwards. … The first root syllable has a special prominence, bearing stress and displaying the full inventory of phonemic contrasts, except for three marginal phonemes, (/ŋ, h, ɾ/). … Additionally, the C1 position is where primary stress is located.
5496.loc: p. 6 and p. 9, section 2.1 'Phonological structure of noun and verb roots' (table (2) lists 'Primary stress' under sigma-1)
5496.idn: Name in the source: Mpyemo; family in the source: Bantu A.80

tn.quote: Mpyemo has three phonetic pitch levels, but only two underlying tone heights: high and low. Two of the phonetic pitch levels are produced by unchanged high and low tones. The third is generated by a high tone raising (HTR) rule, where a high tone is raised to the “super-high” level when followed by a low tone. … Noun melodies consist of two tones per noun, regardless of the number of syllables in the noun. … Mpyemo nouns are thus divided into four major groups: H, L, H(L) and LH; and one minor group: HL.
tn.cite: Festen, Bradley D. 2018. Phonological Sketch of the Mpyemo Language. Bangui: ACATBA (Association Centrafricaine pour la Traduction de la Bible et l'Alphabétisation) & SIL International, SIL Central African Republic Service Group, November 2018. iv + 100 pp. (section 4 'Tone', pp. 26-31; Appendix B c. 1000-item tone-marked wordlist). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

tn.note: Two underlying tones, high and low, as word melodies (nouns H, L, H(L), LH, rare HL); a raising rule gives a third surface level, super-high; floating low tones; stress on the first root syllable.

tn.quote: This paper presents the Ngie (spoken in the Grasslands area of Cameroon) noun classes and tone system. Most Ngie nouns have a V,-C,(G)V,(C,) shape. The second vowel can have one of the following six tone shapes: low with downgliding before pause L [—_], low level L° [ —_], mid level [ —], high H [~ J], falling F [ ~] and rising R [ _~]. Out of the twelve theoretical tonal combinations, only two patterns are lacking: mid followed by level low and mid followed by rising tone.

tn.translation: Xinping Yi has 35 initials, 18 finals and 3 tones, with a very regular tense/lax opposition; the system is: ... Tones (3): tone 1 = 33, tone 2 = 21, tone 3 = 55. Kết quả cho thấy hệ thống thanh điệu tiếng Nùng Xuồng có tính khu biệt rõ ràng, được tổ chức theo cặp đối lập cả về âm vực (cao - thấp) và âm điệu (bằng - trắc), đồng thời phản ánh đầy đủ các dạng vận động của thanh điệu hình tuyến như đi lên, đi xuống, bằng phẳng hay gãy khúc.
tn.translation: Nùng Xuồng and Vietnamese both have a 6+2 structure: 6 tones in non-closed syllables and 2 tones only in closed syllables. … the article has established that the tone system of Nùng Xuồng comprises six basic tones and two checked (nhập) tones. The results show that the Nùng Xuồng tone system is clearly distinctive, organised in opposed pairs both in register (high - low) and in contour (level - oblique), and at the same time reflects all the movement types of linear tone: rising, falling, level or broken.
tn.cite: Nguyễn Phương Linh & Nguyễn Ngọc Bình. 2025. Hệ thống thanh điệu tiếng Nùng Xuồng (tại thôn Thăm Noọng, xã Tát Ngà, huyện Mèo Vạc, tỉnh Hà Giang). Từ điển học & Bách khoa thư 2025(5): 7-13.

tn.quote: (25) a. surface contrasts i. three tone heights (H, M, L) ii. a level L˚ tone which contrasts with L only before pause iii. falling contours: HM, HL, ML iv. no rising contours, with one exception (ncìí ‘chief’s house’) … from the presence of HM, HL, and ML contours, it is obvious that Oku tone cannot be analyzed as privative. … I will now suggest that the underlying system is /H/ vs. /L/ in Oku, and that all M tones are derived, as is the contrast between L˚ and L.
tn.cite: Hyman, Larry M. 2014. How to study a tone language, with exemplification from Oku (Grassfields Bantu, Cameroon). Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 525-562.

tn.note: Two underlying tones, /H/ vs /L/; surface H, M, L, a level L˚ and falling HM, HL, ML contours are derived by rule (M = H lowered after L); floating H and L tones; noun roots /H, L, HL, LH/.
